title: Employment Rights Act 1996, sections 1 to 3: statement of initial employment particulars
source: Employment Rights Act 1996 (c. 18), sections 1 to 3, the revised text on legislation.gov.uk with the amendments in force from 6 April 2020 (S.I. 2018/1378 and S.I. 2019/731). Read 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-09.
note: A drafting check, not legal advice: the scripted rules read whether a particular is there.

rules.text: The particulars are in one document given no later than the first day of work; pensions, collective agreements and training may follow within two months.
The statement names the employer and the worker.
It gives the date the employment began and, for an employee, the date continuous employment began.
The other particulars are given as at a stated date no more than seven days before the statement.
Pay gives the scale or rate or how it is worked out, and the intervals at which it is paid.
Hours give the normal working hours, the days of the week, and whether and how they vary.
Holidays, public holidays and holiday pay are given precisely enough to work out the entitlement, including accrued holiday pay when the job ends.

Sickness and sick pay, and any other paid leave, are given; from 6 April 2026 Statutory Sick Pay is paid from the first full day of sickness absence (Employment Rights Act 2025 ss. 10 and 11). A statement of the right to join a trade union is planned from 1 January 2027 and is not in force on 2026-10-20; a start on or after that date is warned.
Pensions and pension schemes are given.
Any other benefits the employer provides are given.
The notice the worker must give and is entitled to receive is given, or a reference to the law or agreement that sets it.
The job title or a short description of the work is given.
Employment not meant to be permanent gives its expected length or, for a fixed term, its end date.
Any probationary period is given with its length and conditions.
The place of work is given or, when it varies, that fact and the employer's address.
Collective agreements that directly affect the terms are named, with who made them when the employer did not.
Work outside the UK for more than a month gives the period, the currency of pay, any extra pay or benefits for it, and the terms of the return.
Training the employer provides, the part of it the worker must complete, and any required training the worker pays for are given.
Where there is nothing to state under a head, the statement says so.
Any other paid leave is given, or the statement says there is none.

A note gives the disciplinary rules and procedure, to whom the worker appeals a disciplinary or dismissal decision and brings a grievance, and how, and any further steps (rules on health and safety at work aside).

Only sick pay, other paid leave, pensions and training may be given by pointing to another reasonably accessible document, and notice by pointing to the law or a collective agreement; every other particular is stated.
